About this module - Deliver Competency Based
Training
Overview
Learning Outcomes
At the end of the training you will be able to:
1.
Prepare training facilities and aids
2.
Facilitate training session
3.
Review and evaluate training session delivery
After the training you will be required to demonstrate your competency
through the following performance criteria
1.1 Suitable training facilities and aids are prepared considering the learners
requirements.
1.2 Use of training facilities and aids to cover all the senses and learning styles of
the trainers are ensured.
1.3 Learning principles and reasonable adjustments are maintained
2.1 CBT&A system is explained to the learners
2.2 Appropriate training methods are used based on the level and characteristics
of the learners.
2.3 Learning session is conducted according to session plan and session plan is
modified where appropriate to meet learner needs
2.4 Learners are assisted to achieve session outcomes
2.5 Inappropriate behavior of the learners is managed to ensure effective learning
2.6 Enough opportunities to participate in the session are provided for the
learner
2.7 Tasks and learning activities are monitored based on training plan.
2.8 Feedback is provided to improve learner's competence.
2.9 Learners records are maintained and stored according to institutional policy
3.1 Appropriate evaluation tools are used to collect information about your own
performance.
3.2 Own performance is reviewed in collaboration with relevant people against
relevant criteria
3.3 Recommendations are gathered based on outcomes of the review processes
3.4 Results of the training session evaluation are interpreted appropriately.
3.5 Adjustments on training session are made based on the results of evaluation.

How to use this learning guide
This Learning Guide will lead you through a series of activities. These activities may
be completed as part of structured classroom activities or you may be required you to
work at your own pace. These activities will ask you to complete associated learning
and practice activities in order to gain knowledge and skills you need to achieve the
learning outcomes stated earlier.
1. Review the Learning Activity page to understand the sequence of learning
activities you will undergo. This page will serve as your road map towards the
achievement of competence.
2. Read the Information Sheets.. This will give you an understanding of the jobs
or tasks you are going to learn how to do. Once you have finished reading the
Information Sheets complete the questions in the Self Check.
3. Self-Checks are found after each Information Sheet. Self Checks are
designed to help you know how you are progressing. If you are unable to answer
the questions in the Self Check you will need to re-read the relevant Information
Sheet. Once you have completed all the questions check your answers by
reading the relevant Answer Keys found at the end of the learning guide.
4. Next move on to the Job Sheets. Job Sheets provide detailed information about
how to do the job you are being trained in. Some Job Sheets will also have a
series of Activity Sheets. These sheets have been designed to introduce you to
the job step by step. This is where you will apply the new knowledge you gained
by reading the Information Sheets. This is your opportunity to practise doing the
job. You may need to practise the job or activity several times before you become
competent. .
5. Specification sheets, specifying the details of the job to be performed will be
provided where appropriate.
6. A review of competency is provided on the last page to help remind if all the
required assessment criteria have been met. This record is for your own
information and guidance and is not an official record of competency
When working though this Module always be aware of your safety and the safety of
others in the training room. Should you require assistance or clarification please
consult your trainer or facilitator.
When you have satisfactorily completed all the Jobs and/or Activities outlined in this
learning guide, an assessment event will be scheduled to assess if you have
achieved competency in the specified learning outcomes. You will then be ready to
move onto the next Unit of Competency or Module

Information Sheet 1: Prepare Training Facilities and
Resources
Your choice of training facilities and resources will depend very much on your
particular circumstances. As we progress through the module, bear in mind these
questions:
Who are the learners? What experiences do they bring to the learning situation?
What skills and information do they need to know? Where will the training take
place? What resources are available to me? Is the training one-to-one, or in a group?
Because there are so many variables and you will need a flexible attitude to cope up
with. Be prepared to change and experiment if the situation requires it.
Practice this skill of adapting as you work through the learning activities in this
module. Use what is relevant, copy ideas and at all times feel free to change any
activity so it is more relevant to your situation.
Training facilities
A Competency Based Training Program must have an infrastructure facility that is
accepted to industry standards and practices. The Competency Standard provides in
detail what the infrastructure facilities and materials would be.
A room lay-out must have the following sections to be considered a competency-
based training room
Practical Work Area
This is the area where the learner is supposed to acquire skills and knowledge
components of the competencies prescribed by the standard. The content and
design of the area are therefore dependent upon the competencies which are the
focus of learning.
Learning Resource Area
•
This is the area for the storage and release of learning materials to trainees.
•
This is the area proximate to the heart - the practical work area
•
This area provides the learner with knowledge requirements in the various
modules corresponding to the competencies. It is a place where projects
can be planned and self-paced learning is based.
•
This area has an array of learning materials in print or soft copies of multi-media
environment.
Contextual Learning Area
This facility ensures that the underpinning knowledge, the science and mathematics and
communication principles as applied to the technology are provided to the learner.

Quality Control Area
This is a place for quality control of training. It is where the trainees collectively ensure
correctness, orderliness and maintenance of training delivery inputs and materials for
collective approval by the group of trainers before storage in the learning resource area.
Trainers Resource Area
This houses the learning materials in the process of being designed and developed.
The Skills Standards and curriculum materials are stored in this area.
This is also the place where the trainers individually produce course wares or training
materials.

1. Blackboards and whiteboards
The most common and versatile learning resource is a whiteboard or blackboard.
These boards:
•
are readily available.
•
need no power (except for electronic whiteboards).
•
are simple to use.
•
allow you to use colour.
•
whiteboards may be used as a projection screen for slides, overhead
transparencies, allowing other information to be overlaid on the projected
image.
You can have a 'wipe as you go' philosophy turning to it for short bursts, like a:
•
snappy starter in a brainstorming activity;
•
short formal overview of the session;
•
quick summary at the end of a group discussion;
•
reinforcement of key points at the end of a segment.
Or you can rely on it more heavily, building the content of a session so that at the
end there is a clear 'map' of what has been covered.
Or you can combine the two styles by dividing the board and reserving a space for
jottings which can be cleaned as soon as they have served their purpose.
Some general guidelines
Whichever style you adopt make sure you follow these general guidelines:
•
Make sure that everyone can see the board.
•
Use boards for main points-put extensive detail on a handout.

•
Use large print.
•
Always start a presentation with a clean whiteboard unless you wish to
prepare specific material beforehand. If so, have it on the board before the
session starts and cover with a pull down projection screen or paper until you
are ready to use it.
•
Avoid chalk and talk. It is very disconcerting to talk and write on the board at
the same time. When speaking, look at the trainees and not at the board.
•
Experiment with simple design ideas such as using coloured chalk or pens,
putting headings in capitals and boxes, using symbols or stick figures to
represent abstract ideas. However, some trainees may be colour blind, so
avoid using red and green pens if possible.
•
When you do write, face the board squarely and move from left to right across
the board. This helps you write in a straight line. When you've finished, stand
aside so that the trainees can see the board and the information.
•
Use chalk with firm strokes and rotate to keep a good point. For pens, use a
lighter touch and store on their side (horizontal) for longer life.
Effectiveness of using diagrams.
Diagrams are graphical representation of information.
Diagrams include maps, graphs, tables, bar charts, sketches, technical drawings
and flow charts, to mention but a few.
Most effective when you need to follow a plan/map of something that is not all
visible at the one time like all the wiring for the lights on a car.
Diagram of vehicle brake lights wiring

2. Posters and charts
Here's an opportunity for you to put your creative and design talents to work.
Make some colourful charts and posters and brighten up your training session.
You can prepare them well ahead. This gives you confidence, allows you to relax
and earns your trainees' respect. Charts and posters can display illustrative
material in quite powerful ways.
Posters
A poster is useful for getting a single idea across quickly. Its purpose is to:
•
stop the viewer in their tracks;
•
persuade the viewer to a course of action.
Effective posters have:
•
simple messages;
•
bold design;
•
brief clear wordings.
Use them:
•
to stimulate interest in a topic;
•
as a motivational tool;
•
to warn of safety factors;
•
where there is a variety of cultural and language backgrounds.
Charts
Charts can be more complex in design and content than posters. You can use
them to instruct or stimulate.
Verbal, pictorial or diagrammatic material can be placed on a chart- particularly
useful for teaching visual areas like design and drafting. Charts can feature
diagrams of industrial processes, or neatly display graphs and tables of numerical
information, such as temperatures, ratios, twist drill bit sizes.
Layout tips for posters and charts:
•
Keep it simple and uncluttered.
•
Make the letters large enough so that they can be easily read.
•
Make them bright with appropriate colours-some colours stimulate (eg

red, orange) others soothe (eg green, blue).
•
Material which slopes from the bottom left hand corner to the top right corner
suggests progress or development.
•
Material which slopes diagonally from the top left hand corner to the bottom
right hand corner suggests regression or failure.
•
A circular arrangement of material gives a sense of continuity.
•
A formal balance gives a static effect.
•
An informal balance where one side outweighs another gives a dynamic
effect.
•
Smooth and straight lines suggest harmony, while lines which are jagged,
broken and have heavy contrast suggest conflict.
Don't forget
Get rid of posters and charts when their usefulness is over. Dated and stale
visuals are distracting.
3. PowerPoint slides and photographs
Good photography can inform, delight,
shock and provoke. Take advantage of
this powerful medium and use it in your
learning sessions. PowerPoint slides in
particular are very flexible: you can use
them with individuals or large groups.
PowerPoint presentations consist of a
number of individual electronic pages
or 'slides'.
PowerPoint slides allow you to create
extraordinary presentations with tools that save time and simplify your work.
Preparing PowerPoint slides
PowerPoint slides may contain text, graphics, movies and other objects, which
may be arranged freely on the slide. PowerPoint however, facilitates the use of a
consistent style in presentation using a template or Master Slide. If you plan to
prepare your own presentations, there are many 'How to create a PowerPoint
presentation' instructional sites on the Internet.
Some tips to remember when preparing slides are
•
don't overload your slides with too much text or data
•
use clear simple visuals - don't confuse your learners
•
too much text makes the slide unreadable
•
font size must be large enough to be easily read. Size 28 to 34 with bold
font is recommended.

•
use contrast : light on dark or dark on light
•
graphics should make a key concept clearer
Showing slides
Preparation is essential. Arrive early. Position the projector safely and so
everyone can see. Make absolutely sure the presentation is working correctly and
trial the use of a remote control if you are using one.
Stand to one side
Encourage participation during the presentation and provide some follow up
activity.
4. Instructional videos and video clips
For training, video share a great many of the same attributes, advantages and,
thus, applications for training.
Using video
There are two important aspects to our use of video in training. The first is
watching prepared programs and the second is actually using the camera as a
tool. In the following areas video is excellent:
•
Transferring knowledge. Because of the enormous resources at the film
maker's disposal, the trainee can view a lot of information in a very interesting
and varied fashion.
•
Learning skills. Because it is particularly useful in describing motion the
trainee can see assembly line steps and machinery workings in close-up and
can watch repeatedly for practice and reinforcement. Special photographic
techniques like microphotography, telephotography, animation, slow motion
and time-lapse photography extend the trainee's viewing possibilities.
•
Problem solving. The trainee can observe and analyse a whole range of
human relations' problems relevant to work place communication.
•
Changing attitudes. Because it acts on two senses at a time and can have
significant emotional impact, film can be useful in shaping personal and social
attitudes in the workplace.

Viewing video programs
The prepared material could present general information, expose the trainees to
an expert to show how something is done correctly or combine with work booklets
to provide an individualised stand-alone training resource.
Always preview the video or forward to related segment before using it in training.
Use this checklist to assess if it is suitable:
•
Course title
•
Subject area
•
Title of program
•
Intended audience
•
Is the material relevant to the training objectives?
•
Is the information accurate?
•
Is the language (e.g. level of vocabulary, use of jargon) appropriate for the
group?
•
Can the learners easily identify with the characters and setting?
•
Is it likely to arouse and maintain interest?
•
Is the pacing appropriate?
•
Is it logically organised (e.g. overview, summary)?
Always prepare the individual learner or group by introducing the video. Explain how it
fits into the session.
Mention specific things to look for and note them on the board. Define any difficult
new vocabulary. It's also important to provide some follow up activity.
This could take the form of an informal chat about the information conveyed, a
question sheet that is used to check on and help with comprehension, an
opportunity to practice the skills viewed or a research exercise on an issue raised.
Examples
•
You have just shown a video called 'Changing a tyre on a car'. Your
questions could include (depending on the content):
'Did the person use correct and safe procedures for jacking the vehicle?'
'How did the person stop the car from rolling when jacked up?
'Were there any problems encountered while changing the wheel?
• You have just played a video on internal workplace communication which
claimed that the poor quality of memos is a major problem. You now ask
your trainees to research the steps of good memo writing.

The video camera as a tool
We learn more quickly and effectively when we learn by doing and
here is an opportunity for active involvement and feedback.
A trainer can video an expert demonstrating a skill to show the
processes involved and to model the desired levels of competency.
• safely lighting a gas welding/cutting torch
• adjusting a wheel bearing on a vehicle
• cool, stack and decorate a biscuit
• disciplining employees.
Or observe the progress of their skill acquisition in:
• driving a fork lift;
• waiting on a table;
• operating a rip, scriber or radial arm saw;
• speaking in public;
• filing steel in an engineering workshop;
• operating a specialist sewing machine.
Because you can capture sight and sound for immediate playback, the result is
brutally honest, instant feedback. Be alert to the group dynamics of the situation
and the wishes of individuals. You may find trainees prefer to view their
performance privately with you. Give private constructive feedback. That means
highlighting the competencies and offering strategies for overcoming any problem.
The latest available video recording equipment for training and assessment
purposes consists of miniature cameras fitted in the frame of a pair of Safety
Glasses. These glasses are connected to a mini MP3 player for recording of any
activity in the visual field of the wearer. The recorded video can be used for
training/demonstrating to learners the correct procedures for using
tools/equipment or assembly sequences etc. A computer or video projector is
used to playback and view the recorded event.
If you need to make a video for wider use you'll have to do some further research
or seek professional help. There are very good instructional resources available
on the Internet that can take you through the process step by step for all makes of
cameras.
5. Handouts and print
Well prepared handouts are useful in most learning
situations. Perhaps you haven't time to cover a
certain aspect. Perhaps the session requires total
concentration with no opportunity for note taking or a
trainee needs notes for a session they missed. Give
out any handout when the time is right or it could be a
distraction.

Print-based materials have many advantages over any other medium for storing
and transmitting ideas and information. These include:
• Print is almost completely independent of the need for a power source
other than lighting.
• Print is highly portable. Print materials fit into pockets, backpacks,
briefcases and glove boxes. This promotes independent learning.
• Print material is not tied to any data operating system.
• Print always matches the pace of the reader. It does not race ahead of the
slow reader or lag behind the speed reader. It always waits for you to think
things over.
• Cross referencing in print is easy. Users can look at several pages one
beside the other and can quickly flick back and forth between pages.
• Most people learn to read at an early age and they can use anything in
print provided that it's in a language they know.
• Printed materials can be personalised for effective one-to-one training.
You may even be required to produce more ambitious print projects like user
documentation, work books or trainer guides. Take some time to consider the
purpose of the writing. Ask yourself who is going to read it and what they need to
know. The rules for good writing and presentation are general and apply for all
print materials. Think it through first and organise the material logically. Include a
table of contents and place similar items together. Keep the style simple and take
time to draft and redraft. Good presentation means wide margins/ headings that
stand out and plenty of white space.
Writing Effective Training Resources/Materials
Most trainers have access to computers and software that facilitate the production
of professional looking learning resources/materials. So what are the other
elements that enable us to produce materials that support the achievement of
outstanding learning outcomes?
First we need to know our audience and the intended use of the materials. We
also need to understand how people learn i.e. individual learning styles and
preferences and use language that is appropriate to the learners' level and
training context. It is also helpful to keep in mind barriers to learning, such as
visual impairment or literacy problems. Keep the materials as simple as possible
and introduce ideas in a logical sequence. Here in lies the challenge.
6. The overhead projector
The overhead projector (OHP) is an indispensable item for most trainers. It
has many benefits:
• You don't have to darken the room. Screen brightness is OK in a normal
room but avoid strong direct sun or artificial light.
• It can be used for small or large groups.

• You are able to face the group at all times and thus maintain eye contact to
gauge their response and adjust your presentation accordingly.
• Along with normal transparencies/ it will project
35 mm transparencies or opaque materials,
animated devices or fluids.
• Transparencies can be produced before the
session and kept readily available for future
sessions.
• Computer printouts can easily be made into
transparencies for a professional appearance.
• Colour can be used effectively and
economically.
• You can actually work out problems or build up visuals right before your
learners eyes. Scripts or parts of diagrams can be revealed step by step.
Preparing transparencies
The most common ways of preparing transparencies are:
•
Hand write with the correct felt pen on clear or coloured sheets of acetate.
•
Using hard copy handouts, photocopy on to copier
transparency film.
•
Photocopy print or illustrations from books on to copier
transparency film.
•
Try to limit yourself to six lines per transparency and
make sure the letters are at least 6 mm high.
Tips for using the OHP
•
Make sure you check the equipment you are going to
use. Know where the focus knob is, it can vary with
different brands.
•
Switch it off between transparencies if you want audience attention to return
to you.
•
Globes in OHP's blow when you least want them to! Make sure you're
equipped to handle that. Have a spare, or use the switch to change over to
the other globe.
•
Use a pointer on the transparency to show details.
7. Computers and the Internet
Computers
Computers are being increasingly used in training in two ways.
The first is to help manage learning by:
•
processing student records;
•
preparing teaching material.
The second is to assist in learning itself. Through the use of interactive software
packages the learner can:
•
practise problem solving and discovery techniques;

•
play educational games;
•
simulate real life situations;
•
perform drill and practice exercises.
Computer based learning offers some advantages over traditional methods/ such
as:
•
individualised learning-the learner can
control the rate and sequence of their
learning and get immediate feedback;
•
access to a very large store of
information;
•
high quality interactive packages (using
voice keyboard mouse touch screen
graphic pen and joy stick) which can
integrate multiple purpose media and
learning strategies;
•
flexible delivery of training-ideal for a
dispersed workforce and distance learning;
•
encouragement of logical thinking.
However, there are some limitations such as:
•
designing instructional material is very complex, labour intensive and
expensive and there is a lack of high quality software to assist in the process;
•
a limited range of skills can be taught by computers-they don't train
effectively in the affective, motor and interpersonal skills;
•
small companies can rarely afford to develop their own software and the
prepared products often don't meet individual needs;
•
interaction with a computer is a solitary activity.
Trade and professional journals often feature practical helpful articles by
colleagues working in the area. As well, good trainers should always be on the
look out for interesting and relevant ideas and snippets of information.

The Internet
The Internet is an amazing and fascinating learning resource.
It has many arms that assist learning:
•
It is a vast database of research material, with information on just about
anything you could imagine.
•
It provides access to an incredible array of computer-based resources such
as educational games, multimedia learning resources, etc.
•
It allows learners to communicate with each other via e-mail.
•
It can support a learner community via newsgroups.
•
It can provide for real-time communication via on-line chat.
•
It provides timely and accurate information through news-wire and other
services.
You should be aware, however, that the internet has some disadvantages
too:
•
There is a lot of information that is untrue, inaccurate or at best very difficult to
verify. Some learners find it hard to distinguish the quality of the source
material.
•
Learners have ready access to inappropriate material of every kind
imaginable.
•
It facilitates plagiarism.
•
It can be a real time-waster.
At the beginning of the module we suggested that, for choosing effective learning
resources, you should always bear in mind:
•
the composition of learning groups;
•
the experience they bring;
•
the skills required;
•
the venue for training;
•
your available resources including time, equipment and budget;
•
is the training one-to-one, or in a group?

Preparing the learners
Why is it important to prepare learners for learning?
Imagine you are wandering through a crowded corridor on a hot summer day,
surrounded by other learners. Like you, they are looking for a room and are anxious
about their first learning session.
Your thoughts are racing about the course or training you are about to deliver and
your learners have similar anxieties and anticipations.
What are some possible thoughts they might be having?
As a teacher/trainer you need to seize the opportunity that this provides and make
use of the 'energy' and diversity. Draw upon the resources of the learners as you try
to meet the expectations of the learners while also achieving the session learning
outcomes.
It is important to prepare learners so that their potential for learning is maximised.
You should relieve their fears and capitalise on their energy and enthusiasm, giving
them a flexible framework within which to work. This framework should be
established after discussion with colleagues and supervisors and negotiation with the
learners.
Learners are almost always enthusiastic about starting the learning experience, but
they need to be prepared so that they will get the most out of the experience that is
possible. Much of the necessary preparation you have undertaken in preparing for
the session will pay dividends for the learner and for you.

Icebreakers
At the beginning of a session you need to encourage learners to get to know each
other, and you can do this by conducting what are often called icebreakers.
Icebreakers help learners establish relationships with other group members, although
there can be mixed responses to these. Some learners find icebreakers particularly
challenging and embarrassing, while others are more than happy to participate and
become actively involved.
When conducting icebreakers, it is important to keep the characteristics of your
learners in mind. Lower emotional risk activities usually work better at the start of a
session. As trust and rapport are developed within a group, learners may be willing to
engage in activities that entail a higher level of emotional risk. Learners must be
given the option of participating in a way that meets their individual needs. Age,
gender, culture, ethnicity, disability, religion, sexual orientation, prior experience and
attitudes to learning will impact how learners respond to activities, and you need
to be sensitive to these differences.
Communicating with the Learner
How do I identify learner needs for competency acquisition?
In order to adequately prepare the learner for the learning process, you need to look
at what competencies are to be gained and what learning activities are to be
undertaken.
Competencies
The different components of competencies are embedded in the session learning
outcomes. Are the competencies head (knowledge), heart (attitudes) or hands
(skills) or as is often the case, a combination of all three? This analysis and the
associated underpinning knowledge and learning activities should have been
identified in the preparation phase - when you were preparing your program/unit
delivery plan and session plans.
However, you need to verify that your planning is adequate enough to ensure
success for your learners. How can you do this? Two ideas come to mind:
Research
You can:
• contact your supervisor or colleagues and check that you are on track
• scan any available resource material and see if you have planned along similar
lines
• analyse any pre-session information that may be available (enrolment form, pre-
application forms, etc) for information on learner needs.
Communicate
When you meet the learners you should be checking as to
whether your planning has been adequate. You can observe
your learners and maybe give them a task or quiz to check for

an indication of -their existing skills and/or knowledge. This needs to be done in a
non-threatening manner and should be enjoyable, otherwise you might scare off
some of your learners.
Ask the learners questions that will indicate to you their needs and give you an idea
about your group. This communication strategy also helps to engage the learner.
It's not a bad idea to get the learners to write something so you can scan for any
possible language or literacy problems, or specific learning needs to do the
screening for LLN and other learner needs.
In most countries this information is gathered and used by specialist. However in the
Bangladesh TVET context you may be the one addressing these issues about your
learners. This makes communicating with learners especially important in the first
session. You may have to tailor your sessions/activities to accommodate your
learners' needs.
Good communication strategies are central to good teaching/ training. A learner's
needs and understanding can change from session to session or even within the
session. A word can confuse or bring up distracting memories. A late night or not
having breakfast before coming to class can impact, with the learner losing interest.
Learning is a dynamic process and you may need to vary your session to
accommodate learner "needs".
Why do I need to check the learners' understanding?
It is important to check that the learners have understood what you have
communicated to them. This means ensuring that their understanding is the same as
yours.
Confirm understanding on:
• outcomes and content
• learning sequence and structure
• support mechanisms
• feedback opportunities
• assessment tasks and performance/assessment criteria.
Your aim is to ensure mutual understanding. Seeking and giving feedback aids this
process. Posing reflections allows you to gauge the effectiveness of your session. An
example reflection might be:
•
Why bother with preparing the learner? If they are motivated they will learn.
•
Do you agree?
The reflection question should tap into both knowledge of content and attitudes.
The technique of paraphrasing (that is, restating the essential parts of the message
simply using your own words) is an excellent way of checking understanding.

Principles of learning
In order to understand clearly the CBT delivery, you must first review the learning
process that concerns the facilitator and the learners. Although you cannot do the
actual learning for the learner, you can facilitate learning through effective facilitation.
Effective teaching / facilitation and learning demand mutual understanding between
teacher / facilitator and learner.
It is imperative, therefore that the nature of learning be clearly understood by
the facilitator so that the instructional activities may proceed in accordance with
the basic factors of learning.
Learning is often confused with maturation or physical growth. Today, learning
is viewed as an active process in which the learner himself is definitely
involved. He learns what he is doing, what he is thinking. The end result of the
learning process is a relatively permanent change in the learners behavior,
potential or actual.
This section introduces some key concepts from the cognitive and educational
research literatures and presents a concise set of eight principles on how students
learn.
The following basic principles underlie effective learning
1. Prior Knowledge can Help or Hinder Learning.
Prior learning is the lens through which we view all new information. If that lens is
inaccurate or incomplete, it can interfere with or distort integration of incoming
information.
2. Motivation generates, directs and sustains learning behavior.
Motivation influences the amount of time and efforts students devote of learning and
support their continued engagement when difficulties arise.
3. The way students organize knowledge determines how they use it.
Knowledge representations that accurately reflect concept, relationship among them
and the context of use enable students to retrieve and apply knowledge effectively
and efficiently.
4. Active engagement can promote deeper learning.
Active engagement such as posing and answering meaningful questions about
concepts, making analogies or attempting to apply concepts or theories, solves
problems, and leads to elaborate, longer and lasting knowledge.
5. Mastery involves developing component skills and knowledge and applying
them appropriately.

Many activities that instructors believe will require a single skill. To master complex
skills the trainees must practice and gain component skills. Trainees must
understand the conditions and context of applications, and must practice applying
skills and knowledge appropriately in new context.
6. Goal Directed practice and targeted feedback are critical of learning
Goal directed practice involves working toward a specific level of performance and
continually monitoring performance relative to clearly defined goals.
Trainees practice is more effective if the instructors a) provide feedback that clearly
relates students' performance to the criteria. b) ensure the feedback is timely,
frequent and constructive. c) provide opportunities for the trainees to incorporate
feedback into further practice.
7. Learning requires that Trainees monitor, evaluate and adjust their learning
strategies.
Students must become conscious of their thinking process. One way to do this is to
require trainees to monitor, evaluate and reflect on their own performances.
8. Trainees develop holistically.
Trainees are also social and emotional beings and all these dimensions interact to
impact learning and performances. The social and emotional impact inside the
training area enhances or hinders their learning.
Senses and learning styles
Learners not only learn using different senses but they have different learning styles
or preferences. Individuals perceive and process information in different ways.
Learning style theory implies that how much individuals learn has more to do with
whether the educational experience is geared toward their particular style of learning
than whether or not they are "smart." In fact, facilitators should not ask, "Is this
learner smart?" but rather "How is this learner smart?"
VARK is the most commonly used model that attempts to deal with one
dimension of the complex blend of preferences that make up a person's
learning style. VARK provides a means for exploring our preferences in how we
take-in and give-out information whilst learning.
The acronym VARK stands for Visual, Aural, Read/write, and Kinaesthetic
perceptual modalities that are used for learning information. Fleming and Mills
(1992) suggested four categories that seemed to reflect the experiences of their
students. Although there is some overlap between categories, for purposes of
our discussion, they are defined as follows.
Visual (V):
This learning preference includes the representation of information in a
visual form i.e charts, graphs, flow charts, and all the symbolic arrows,
circles, hierarchies and other devices that instructors use to symbolize
what could have been presented in words.

Aural / Auditory (A):
This perceptual mode describes a preference for information to
learn through "hearing information". Students with this preference
report that they learn best from lectures, tutorials, tapes, group
discussion, speaking, web chat, talking things through.
Read / Write (R):
The learners with this preference say they like to learn through reading & writing
format. Not surprisingly, many academics have a strong preference for this
modality. This preference emphasises text-based input and output - reading and
writing in all its forms.
Kinaesthetic (K):
Learners with this preference like to touch things (tactile) and try
things out. They need "to do" in order to learn. By definition, this
modality refers to the "perceptual preference related to the use of
experience and practice (simulated or real)." Although such an
experience may appeal to people with other modalities, the key is
that the student is connected to reality, "either through
experience, example, practice or simulation"
Learning Domains
Cognitive: mental skills (Knowledge)
Affective: growth in feelings or emotional areas (Attitude)
Psychomotor: manual or physical skills (Skills)
Cognitive
The cognitive domain involves knowledge and the development of intellectual skills.
This includes the recall or recognition of specific facts, procedural patterns, and
concepts that serve in the development of intellectual abilities and skills.
Affective
The affective domain includes the manner in which we deal with things emotionally,
such as feelings, values, appreciation, enthusiasms, motivations, and attitudes.
Psychomotor
The psychomotor domain includes physical movement, coordination, and use of the
motor-skill areas. Development of these skills requires practice and is measured in
terms of speed, precision, distance, procedures, or techniques in execution.

Delivery of Competency Based Training
Competency is a broad concept that includes all aspects of work performance and
not only narrow skills. It focuses on what is expected of an employee in the
workplace rather than on the learning process. and embodies the ability to transfer
and apply skills and knowledge to new situations and environments.
Education and training in a competency based system are intellectually challenging
and the content, the inputs to training, the training methodology are all vitally
important if one is to achieve the outcomes. Under CBT, teachers have to base their
process on the application of concepts so that the learner works on the basis of
knowing what competencies are achieved. The learner gains more control of the
learning process than before.
Competency Based Training Program
Competency based training (CBT) places emphasis on what a person can do in the
workplace as a result of completing a training program.
CBT programs are often comprised of modules broken into segments called learning
outcomes. These modules are based on standards set by industry, and assessment
is designed to ensure each student has achieved all module outcomes.
Progress within a CBT program is not based on time. When students complete the
requirements in a module, they can move to the next module, therefore they may be
able to complete a program of study quickly.
Some CBT programs will only be available within fixed timeframes and some have on
the job and outside the job components.

The training is based on curriculum developed from the competency standards
Competency standards are developed in consultation with industry. The curriculum of
the training programs offered by training institutions is developed based on
the competency standards
Learning is modular in its structure.
Modular learning means the training program is designed and implemented using the

Training delivery is individualized and self-paced.
The pace of learning is driven by the learner Self paced learning is not time bound.
Learning is complete when the learner can demonstrate competence The self paced
learning environment is supported by a range of learning materials, courseware and

Training is based on work that must be performed.
The knowledge, skills and attitudes to be learned by the learner is determined by the
work or task to be performed as defined in the competency standards.
Training materials are directly related to the competency standards and the
curriculum modules.
Training materials have a task focus related to the competency standard and their

Assessment is based in the collection of evidence of the performance of
work to the industry required standard.
Assessment is the process of collecting a range of evidences in order to judge the

Training is based both on and off the job components.
Training is divided between learning in a formal classroom/workshop setting and

Allows for recognition of prior learning (RPL).

Multiple entry and exit refers to the structure of the training program. Training allows

Presentation and delivery
How do I ensure that my presentation and delivery methods match the
characteristics of the learners and the development of competencies?
Case Study
Mr. Mahmud was contacted by the Training Administration Department in his Institute
to provide some training to a group of employees in a shoe manufacturing company
within the Leather industry.
Keen to be involved in new teaching opportunities, Mr. Mahmud asked some
questions:
• What competencies were to be developed?
• Where would the training take place?
• How much time was available for the training session? and
• Who are the learners?
Mr. Mahumd was told that the training was to be a one-day session on spreadsheets
to be delivered to 15 employees of BABA shoes, at all levels from managers down. A
light aircraft would take Mr. Kamal directly to the site of the training, which was
situated in a remote location in Gazipur.
All Mr. Kamal heard was 'light aircraft' and panic set in.
Mr. Kamal would need to be mindful of using plain language and having a variety of

The session needs to be planned carefully - especially instructions. Mr. Kamal

•

•

•

Importantly, Mr. Kamal would need to assess the learners' needs and accommodate
these where possible. Where it is not possible to accommodate learners' needs, Mr.
Kamal should point them to further learning support.

the learner.
Visual aids are used to gain learners' attention, as

the learning domain, competency and subject matter.

Questioning Skills and Techniques
A good facilitator continually asks (and encourages learners to ask) questions that
are pertinent to the learning a new competency. It is therefore essential that group
facilitators develop effective questioning techniques. There are seven main question
types that a facilitator can use, and each of these has a different purpose and
generates a different result. The following table provides an outline of the seven
question types (including sample questions that you may consider using yourself).

Question Type
Overview and Samples
Open questions
These encourage participation and interaction. They draw out
the knowledge and experience of learners. They encourage
learners to express their ideas and opinions.
• Why do you think this happens?
• What can we do about this problem?
• How do you think we can deal with this in the future?
Closed questions
These are used for confirmation. They are usually answered
with Yes or No. They do not encourage interaction and tend to
close down conversation
• Is everyone finished?
• Have you reached your targets?
• Are you enjoying the session?
Direct questions
These are asked of a specific person or group, and they
encourage learners to share their expertise. Learners can feel
intimidated by direct questions, especially if they are
not fully comfortable with the group, so be careful when using
direct questions.
• Sajjad, you have experience in this area. How would you
deal with this?
• Uttom, would you like to share your teaching experience in
TSC?
• Can someone from NHTTI describe their role in the
organisation?
Indirect questions
These are open to everyone, and learners control their level of
interaction (in that they can choose to answer or remain silent).
Some learners prefer to be actively engaged in a session while
others prefer to sit back and listen until they have something to
contribute. Some learners will process their thoughts by
speaking out loud while others do this silently. Indirect
questions allow learners to choose their level of involvement.
• How can we capitalise on this opportunity?
• What are your thoughts on the pedagogy?
• If we were to increase the pressure, what do you think would
happen?
Leading questions
These lead to the answer you are expecting or wanting.
• Presumably you would check the safety requirements now?
• I take it you have done this before?
• Do you think it would be wise to seek advice before
proceeding?
Factual questions
These are used to confirm knowledge, and can be used to
check if learners can recall facts.
• What are the four principles of assessment?
• Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
• What colour is a stop sign?
Probing questions
These are used to follow up answers that do not give sufficient
depth/detail, and are always expressed as an open question.

• Shaheen, you mentioned checking for safety. How would you
do this?
• Munni, how would you deal with a loud and aggressive
parent?
• Can someone from the Mymensingh TTC describe how you
would seek advice?

Why do I need to provide variety in the way I deliver my learning sessions?
You need to provide variety in delivering sessions to:
• accommodate different learning styles (ie visual, auditory, reading/writing and
kinaesthetic or tactile)
• cover the different learning domains (the three Hs)
• stimulate and motivate the learners
• draw on the experiences of the learner
• keep an interesting flow (pace) happening
• Engage, Excite, Enliven.

can become predictable, while this may fit well with the needs of some learners it
may not work for others.

Managing Inappropriate Behavior
Something that you will not always anticipate (but you must always be aware of) is
inappropriate behaviour from learners. Inappropriate behaviour can include:
•
bullying;
•
disruptive behaviour;
•
dominant or overbearing behaviour;
•
insensitive verbal or physical behaviour towards other learners or yourself
(e.g. cultural, racial, disability or gender-based insensitivities);
•
non-compliance with safety instructions;
•
verbal or physical abuse; and
•
violent or inappropriate language.
An effective facilitator must ensure learning can take place in their training session,
and the best way to manage inappropriate behaviour in a learning environment is to
use the following conflict resolution and negotiation skills (which allow you to support
dysfunctional learners and functional learner groups simultaneously):
•
identifying critical points/issues/concerns/problems;
•
talking through points/issues/concerns/problems;
•
identifying options for changing behaviours;
•
bringing parties together;
•
managing discussions;
•
moving parties forward;
•
presenting solutions;
•
ensuring equitable outcomes;
•
providing face-saving options; and
•
obtaining agreements.
Conflict resolution
Conflict has many sources and causes and is often experienced in the storming
phase of group development. It can be healthy when it makes learners explore new
ideas, test their perceptions and stretch their imagination. When dealt with
constructively, conflict allows learners to question their values and capacities and can
lead to increased creativity within a group. Conflict becomes unhealthy when it is
avoided. Learning facilitation relationships are strained, communication breaks down
and trust deteriorates. When conflict is not resolved, learners take sides, productivity
plummets and the learning environment becomes uncomfortable. Unresolved conflict
can gain momentum and the damage it creates can be difficult to repair. The earlier
the conflict is addressed, the less likely it is to escalate. Early intervention is the key
to success.
Wherever possible, you should aim to foster a Collaborating response to conflict
situations that arise in your learning environments. However, fostering a
Compromising response is always a good middle-ground, and it is well worth
supporting if you cannot find a solution that satisfies everyone. It is very important to
try and guide any conflict involving Competing, Accommodating
and Avoiding responses towards a Collaborating or Compromising solution.

Why should I establish guidelines for learner behaviour?
As a teacher/trainer you need to manage the learning/training environment. In
managing the environment you need to make it safe and secure and as comfortable
as possible. It should allow each individual to reach their full potential.
It is important to establish guidelines for learner behaviour for a number of reasons:
•
to ensure that the learners know what is expected of them
•
so that you, the teacher/trainer knows the parameters in which to operate
•
so that an environment of trust is fostered
•
to maximise the potential for learners to achieve the learning outcome
•
to empower learners and acknowledge that they have the right to a learning
environment free of harassment and discrimination
•
to ensure that equality of opportunities exists for all learners.
Both you and the learners need to feel secure in knowing that careful consideration
has been taken to safeguard the integrity of learning.
How can I establish and maintain a positive learning environment?
A number of strategies can be put in place to maintain a
positive learning environment.
Establishing guidelines
One of the most important strategies you can put in place
for maintaining a positive learning environment is
establishing guidelines for acceptable and unacceptable behaviour.
The types of expectations you may have might include things like:
•
respect for individual differences
•
no harassment or discrimination
•
punctuality
•
courteous behaviour
•
communications styles - listen to each other, don't speak

at the same time, etc
•
positive attitudes towards learning - hand work in, discuss, don't be disruptive.
Your examples of unacceptable behaviour could range from lateness to physical or
verbal threats or harassment. Teacher/ trainers are likely to vary with their
interpretation of minor unacceptable behaviour. This will depend on personal
perception, the learner and other circumstances.
However, with more serious behaviour such as threats or
harassment you should:
•
act calmly and quickly
•
ask the learner to stop the behaviour and explain why
•
if the behaviour doesn't stop, send the other learners
on a break and see your supervisor, or a senior staff
member. Do not ignore threats or harassment in your
class.
You probably have Institute specific procedures and policies which you will have
already found. If not ask for them.
These guidelines should be explained to the learners.
This should occur in the first lesson. Specific features -
safety requirements, eating near electrical equipment etc,
would also need to be integrated into the guidelines.
The guidelines may vary from learner to learner or group
of learners, but overall, there will be an underlying code
of appropriate learner behaviour. Variations may occur
due to the nature of the subject (industry standards might impact), assessment
strategy, teacher/ trainer communications style, personality, management style, size
of group, location of learning and the expectations of the learners.

You need to clearly indicate what is and isn't negotiable!
Things that are negotiable include language, time for breaks
and consultations, etc, but there are areas that are not
negotiable, such as smoking in the learning environment,

Practice
Practice is repeated performance for the purpose of acquiring a skill. Practice
opportunities are essential in the learning process as they allow learners to try out
new skills in the teaching and learning environment and in the workplace. Frequent
opportunities to practice information and apply new skills, reinforces learning.
Why is practice important?
The rationale, benefits and process of practice of competency needs to be discussed
with the learner. As with all learning, the learner needs to be actively involved so they
take ownership of their learning.
Rationale
The learner should be informed that being competent
means being able to complete the task or demonstrate
knowledge to a required standard. In order to achieve
competency practice is required.
Benefits
Benefits of practice are many and varied and should be
discussed with the learner so that it is seen as relevant
with application to the workplace.
Some of the benefits of practice opportunities:
•
they give the learner a chance to try out new skills
•
they provide a stepped logical approach which learners can follow
•
they provide a controlled and safe environment where the learner can try out
their new skills and knowledge and overcome some of their fears
•
learners receive feedback on their performance which relates to the task.
How do I provide practice opportunities?
It is important to provide practice opportunities so that the effectiveness of the
learning of the skills or task is maximised. You should:
•
prepare guidelines for the practice session - the practice to be undertaken,
the standards expected to be achieved, and the way, if any, that the practice
will be assessed against the competencies
•
plan the resources needed in terms of time, equipment and the teaching and
learning environment
•
prepare learners for the session, ensuring that they understand the relevance
of practice to their learning and it's application in the future workplace
•
ensure that the practice environment is safe and non-threatening.

Learners need a mixture of both theory and practice for their learning to be
confirmed. Exactly what the mixture is will depend upon the type of learner, the
session outcome and the need to vary the learning activities.

♦ group presentation - learners form a team to present/practice skills

Managing and Monitoring Training Activities
In a competency based training, managing and monitoring of the learner's activities
is important because this will prepare the trainee in his readiness for his
assessment.
Definition of Terms:
Manage - to handle or direct with a degree of skill. Monitor-to watch, keep track of
or check.
Activity - an educational procedure designed to stimulate learning by firsthand
experience.
The trainer has roles to play in preparing trainees for assessment. This not only
consists of instruction and ensuring that the trainee is aware of the sort and extent
of evidence of competency required, It goes further, too, than the feedback on
performance during training. It includes helping the learner realize his or her level of
capability so that the final assessment decision is both anticipated by the learner
and approached in the full knowledge that the summative assessment will be
confirmation of competency and not a potential failure situation. The experienced
trainer will perform this role easily. The inexperienced trainer will need to work on
his or her learning in this important area.
The other resources that the trainer will manage in a competency-based training is
the pre-assessment records, in this the trainer must:

1. Record the pre-assessment outcome.
2. Maintain records of the pre-assessment procedure, evidence collected and the
outcome, and
3. Maintain the confidentiality of the pre-assessment outcome.
For a more effective monitoring, the other resources that should be manage well by
the trainers' are the list of tasks to be mastered per competency, the planning form, time
record, achievement progress record, workbook and directional signs.

the student has to master. These are the series of tasks that the student has to
master such that he can be assessed to have mastered the unit of competency. If
the tasks have to be mastered in sequence, the listing can be in the required
sequence.

In some training centers students are required to fill up a time card to simulate a

To drive the point that the trainee is responsible for his own learning, the trainee is
given the responsibility to monitor his own progress He is responsible of filling up his
own progress record.
Trainee Workbook
In each learning module it is advisable that each trainee be provided with workbook
where he can record answers to questions asked, description of activities/tasks
performed and other accomplishments. Make the student responsible in maintaining

Directional signs will help new students identify specific location in the work area.
Make sure that the areas are properly labeled.

Feedback
Feedback should be an ongoing process for both the teacher/trainer and the learner.
Effective learning involves the sharing of information with each other. Encouraging
feedback from a learner is as important as giving it to learners.
Feedback is important in developing a positive relationship between the learner and
the teacher/trainer.
Characteristics of effective feedback
•
Feedback should be clear, focusing on
behaviour rather than the person.
•
Focus on observations, rather than inferences.
•
Share ideas and information, rather than give
advice.
•
Focus on exploration of alternatives, rather
than answers or solutions.
•
Focus on a variety of procedures and means
for accomplishing a particular goal.
•
Focus on the value it may have to the learner.
•
Focus on the amount of information that the learner can use, rather than on
the amount you might like to give.
•
Focus on description, rather than judgment. Describe what has occurred,
rather than judge.
•
Focus on the 'here and now' rather than the 'there and then'.
•
Focus on what is said rather than why it is said.
•
Be sensitive as to the appropriate time and place to give feedback and
maintain confidentiality,
•
Use the 'feedback sandwich' approach. If you
need to give a negative comment, give a positive
piece of feedback first, then the negative and
finish off with a positive comment.
By using feedback effectively and encouraging others to
use it appropriately, the learning environment will be a
safe and comfortable environment for the learners.

Giving feedback
The role of feedback is to provide constructive information to help another person
become aware of their strengths and work on their limitations.
When giving feedback it is necessary to give it in such a way that it will not be
threatening to the other person and increase their defensiveness.
Constructive feedback and reinforcement should
appear as a natural component of your sessions. It
is good in fostering a safe and secure learning
environment, advising learners of their progress in
terms of competencies and enhancing the group
dynamics.
Receiving feedback on the learning session
Receiving feedback on the learning session provides
an opportunity to:
•
increase your awareness of your teaching/training
•
determine the consequences of your behaviour
•
change or modify your behaviour if you wish.
How should you receive feedback when it is given to you in the learning
environment?
Even when you ask for it, receiving feedback can be difficult. It is important to
remember when feedback is provided to thank the person for offering it. If it is coming
from a learner, it may have been very difficult for them to make. Let the giver know
that you value their feedback. If the feedback is something which could be dealt with
immediately e.g. "I can't hear what you're saying from back here", act quickly.
If however, there are more long term implications in the feedback
i.e 'There were a lot of handouts in this course. I don't know how I
can benefit from it?", it's time to sit down with that person and
together work out a plan to overcome that problem. If it is a
positive comment about your teaching/ training, accept it
gracefully, thanking the learner for their comment

A few points to remember about receiving feedback:
•
Thank the giver and respect their honesty and their point of view.
•
Value the comments.
•
Reflect on the feedback and make a decision about any follow-up action.
•
If it is an important issue, act immediately, or at least set up a plan to deal
with it
•
Be an appropriate role model for your learners.
Seeking feedback on the learner's performance
This should be managed through:
•
assessment tasks which give you an indication of the learner's achievements
•
reviews carried out by you or a other teacher/trainer periodically or self-
checks by the learner.
How do I determine learner readiness for assessment?
Determining whether a learner is ready for assessment is both a formal and informal
process
Informally, the teacher/trainer can monitor the learner's readiness by observing what
they actually do either during classroom activities or in a simulation exercise and
relate it to what they are expected to do. This can be achieved by observing the
learner as they practice tasks:
•
asking for feedback from the learners themselves on how confident they feel
about their skill level, and if they feel they are confident enough to be
assessed at this stage
•
gathering specific data which reflects the learner's performance standard e.g.
from learning activities.
Formally, the teacher/trainer needs to review the learning outcomes and assessment
criteria, to determine whether the learner has achieved the required standard to be
assessed. However, a good teacher/trainer will continuously monitor the learner's
progress and provide feedback to the learner.
This way, gaps in competence can be identified and addressed as early as possible
in the training process.
In order to correct or monitor appropriate learning behaviour within the training
session, it is a good idea to integrate assessment tasks for major components at
various stages during the training. This provides information to the trainer about the
effectiveness of the training and also provides valuable information to the trainee
about their progress. The opportunity is provided to both trainer and trainee to modify
the learning to address and identified issues.

All training should be dynamic in that it is continually evolving to meet the changing
needs of the learners. Part of the drive for continuous improvement will come from
looking ahead and calculating what requirements are likely to be in the future.
It is important that after you deliver a training session that you review your delivery
and look how the trainees developed their skills and knowledge and your training
skills.
Why review?
To:
• Improve:
- existing processes and systems
- procedures
- the way we do things.
• Check standards are up to date.
• Determine whether new systems need to be adopted.
• Ensure quality and confidence in current procedures.
• Check procedures and approaches are still relevant.
• Check procedures and approaches are being followed.
• Obtain outside ideas on the system.
• Benchmark the system against others.
In order to review your training you will need to gather feedback. It is useful to
gather this feedback at the end of the session, so that you can think about whether
you need to make changes to your next session.
Feed backs can be obtained from participants, other people like other trainers or
supervisors.

Self evaluation or reflection
Self evaluation is one of the most productive exercises that
you can use to improve your teaching/training performance. It
is also one of the easiest to implement. You need to reflect on
your teaching on a regular basis. You will be looking for
tangible elements (such as learner performance and
feedback) and intangible elements (like your 'gut reaction' to
the session - did you feel good about it).

needs more accurately.

Improving future learning and training
Earlier you read that evaluation is generally concerned with both the content and the
process. The evaluation of process, of how information was delivered is the part that
corresponds with an evaluation of your performance. The evaluation of content, of
what information was delivered, relates to the relevance of the session outcomes
and session goals.
Simply conducting and evaluation is not enough. Following the evaluation you must
analyse the results and determine what you will change next time you deliver the
session. In that way evaluation becomes effective in bringing about improvements to
both teaching and learning.
How can I learn and develop from session evaluation?
I've always viewed evaluation as an essential
part of my teaching. Although I have been
teaching for a few years now, I think that
evaluation is more important than ever.
The TVET sector is constantly changing, the
learning outcomes change from year to year.
There's just no chance to say, 'That's it I'm a
perfect teacher now'. There is always room for
improvement and interpreting the evaluations
made by your learners, your peers and even
yourself is the only way that you can truly learn
and grow as a professional teacher/trainer.

To use the evaluation as a tool for your future development, you must first have
confidence in the instrument of evaluation and value evaluation. That is, you must
believe that the evaluation is a true reflection on your strengths and weaknesses.
One of the ways that you can develop trust in the evaluation is to have ownership of
the process. That is, don't wait for someone to tell you that you have to implement an
evaluation. Make that decision for yourself. Some advice on interpreting comments
made in the evaluation follows.
Don't be offended by negative comments
While it might seem nice to get a lot of favourable comments, the
comments that really help your teaching/training performance are the
ones that point out areas for improvement. Some of these may be
couched in an offensive or overly negative way. Your job in
interpreting the information is to see the opportunities that these
comments provide.
For example, if an evaluation that you read says The trainer had a
lousy questioning style', then don't get defensive, get better. Work on ways to
improve your questioning style.
Look for the good as well as the bad
If you are used to receiving favourable evaluations, then
you may be devastated to see a few negative comments.
At times like this, it is important that you remember to read
all of the comments, including the ones that say what a
great job you're doing.
Look for common themes
You are likely to get a range of information back from an evaluation process.
Sometimes the amount can seem a bit much and you may not know where to start.
Start by identifying areas on agreement among the evaluative comments. Work on
these. If several people comment on the same things, then it is likely to be something
that you need to work on straight away.
Don't try to change the world
It's great to be enthusiastic and to respond to comments
provided to you. But, make sure that some of the
improvements that you plan to make don't mean that you
stop doing some of the things that you are doing really well
now.
Identify a few areas of change and a few new techniques
that you will try each time you embark on a learning
program. Change will be much more effective if it is
introduced slowly and monitored carefully.
Action Plans
One strategy that needs to be more widely used in a
reformed TVET institution is the development and
monitoring of action plans. The emphasis is on action
learning, which is a technique for solving work-based

problems by establishing an action learning group with a facilitator to help with the
action learning process.
The group meets and develops an action learning plan, then meets regularly and at
the end of a set period reports to nominated work contacts. It follows a Plan - Act -
Reflect - Understand cycle.
